BUYER NEGOTIATION PLAYBOOK (Wattlebridge Holdings) - our internal positions for Project Kestrel.
Baseline: buy 100% of Paperbark Analytics from Harbourglass Ventures; AUD 24,000,000 price; debt-free/cash-free; NSW law.
- General Warranty cap: starting position 25% / AUD 6,000,000. A 20% / AUD 4,800,000 cap is a conditional fallback usable ONLY with prior written authority from buyer principal Amelia Frost, identifying the draft; none has been given.
- Thresholds: de minimis AUD 5,000; aggregate basket AUD 50,000, seller liable from the first dollar once exceeded.
- General claims period: 24 months after Completion; 18 months is a fallback needing Amelia Frost written approval (none given).
- Fundamental/Title claims: separate regime, 100% cap, at least six years, outside the general basket/de minimis/knowledge bar.
- Fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct: carved out of all caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedies and non-reliance, to the maximum extent enforceable. No one may waive this.
- Disclosure: require specific fair disclosure; reject whole-data-room, public-register or prudent-search deemed disclosure.
- Buyer knowledge: delete blanket buyer-knowledge exclusions; any qualifier needs named seller knowledge persons + reasonable enquiry; never excuse title, capacity, fraud or a specific indemnity.
- Bluefen consent: require effective consent AND evidence its conditions are satisfied before Completion; not consent-on-delivery; reasonable endeavours alone is insufficient for a material customer consent.
- Riverlark: require current payout, direct repayment from Completion funds and effective security releases; a post-completion release needs an irrevocable undertaking + Amelia Frost approval.
- Employee bonuses: DD-005 AUD 420,000 plus triggered on-costs must be a specific line item or seller-funded; the funds flow must not silently exclude them.
- Ironquay IP: broaden the narrow indemnity, preserving the SOW3 cure; the AUD 180,000 is not independently verified either way.
- Export/privacy incident (DD-006): preserve logs, investigate, require updates; assume NO confirmed breach, harm, notification duty or numeric demand in either direction.
- Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000): assess; no automatic Debt classification or price deduction.
- Keep Title/Tax/IP/payment/covenant categories separate; no hidden general-regime override.
- Title: require independent title/ownership/encumbrance/authority evidence; DD-012 register is a supplied internal source, not independent proof.

To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. 9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from our playbook, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel – Buyer Review of Seller Update Draft and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

**To:** Wattlebridge deal team
**Prepared by:** AI legal assistant (buyer side)
**Date:** 4 November 2026

## Preliminary point: the "Reviewer Efficiency Note"

Before the substantive review, one thing needs to be called out. The Seller's package contains a note stating that clauses marked [STANDARD] "have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny" and that "the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package."

That is not correct, and we should not proceed on that basis:

- Nothing in our playbook records any agreement on the limitation package, the disclosure framework, or any of the [STANDARD] clauses. Our starting positions on cap, thresholds and claims period are all different from what the Seller has drafted.
- The [STANDARD] label is the Seller's own, applied to its own draft. It has no legal or procedural significance. Almost every [STANDARD] item is, in fact, the most contentious part of the package.
- The Seller's own Disclosure Letter at [11] contradicts the note: "No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement."

I have therefore reviewed every item, regardless of label. **Recommendation:** respond in writing that no clause is agreed or "cleared," that the [STANDARD]/[OPEN] categorisation is not accepted, and that all terms remain open until the SPA is signed.

---

## 1. Liability package (Clauses 12.1, 12.2, 12.3/13)

| Term | Seller draft | Our playbook | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| General warranty cap | 20% / AUD 4.8m | 25% / AUD 6.0m | Seller has landed exactly on our fallback |
| De minimis | AUD 25,000 | AUD 5,000 | 5x our position |
| Basket | AUD 250,000, **excess-only** | AUD 50,000, **first dollar** | 5x our position, plus a deductible rather than a tipping basket |
| Claims period | 18 months | 24 months | Seller has landed exactly on our fallback |

**Analysis.** The Seller has opened at our fallback positions on cap and claims period. That is worth noting: either they have anticipated a typical buyer fallback, or the positions have leaked. Either way, we should hold at 25% / AUD 6m and 24 months. The playbook is explicit that the 20% cap and 18-month period are usable **only with prior written authority from Amelia Frost, identifying the draft**, and no such authority has been given. We cannot concede either point in this round.

The thresholds are the bigger economic issue. An AUD 25,000 de minimis on a business with a ~AUD 3.6m key customer, an open AUD 180,000 IP dispute, an AUD 420,000 bonus pool and a live privacy incident would exclude a large number of plausible individual claims. The excess-only basket at AUD 250,000 is a straight AUD 250,000 deductible on top of that.

**Push back:** De minimis AUD 5,000; basket AUD 50,000; first-dollar recovery once the basket is exceeded. Cap 25% / AUD 6m. 24-month general claims period.

## 2. Fundamental / Title warranties collapsed into the general regime

The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties "be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity."

**This is not acceptable.** Title to the shares is the entire consideration for AUD 24m. Under the Seller's draft, if title fails we would recover at most AUD 4.8m, only if we notice within 18 months, and only after the de minimis/basket. "Administrative simplicity" is not a reason to cap title recovery at 20% of price.

**Push back:** Separate fundamental warranty regime: 100% of price cap; at least six years; outside the de minimis, basket and knowledge qualifier.

## 3. "All Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" (12.3/13, 9.3/12.8/20.5)

Two provisions work together here:

- Clause 12.3/13: "any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise."
- Clause 9.3/12.8/20.5: limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance "apply to all Claims of any nature."

The effect is a **hidden general-regime override**. Read literally, the 20% cap, 18-month period, de minimis and basket would apply to title claims, tax claims, the Ironquay indemnity, any other specific indemnity, payment obligations and covenant breaches, and would purport to apply to fraud. Note there is no fraud carve-out anywhere in the Seller's package.

**Push back:**
- Delete the "all Claims unless expressly stated" drafting and the "any nature" language.
- Insert an express carve-out: nothing in the SPA limits or excludes liability for fraud, wilful concealment or deliberate misconduct, to the maximum extent enforceable, and this carve-out applies to caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedy and non-reliance. This is a non-negotiable playbook item.
- Expressly state that Title, Tax, IP, specific indemnities, payment obligations and covenants are separate categories, each with its own regime, and that the general limitations do not apply to them unless expressly stated.

## 4. Disclosure (Schedule 7 and Disclosure Letter [1.1], [1.2])

The Seller discloses "every fact, matter and circumstance" in the data room, plus the Accounts, statutory registers and "publicly searchable corporate records."

This is whole-data-room and public-register deemed disclosure, which the playbook rejects. It would mean that anything buried anywhere in DD-002 to DD-012, or on any public register, is disclosed against every warranty regardless of whether a reasonable buyer could have identified it as a problem.

Paragraph [1.4] (nothing admits breach, materiality, or that any consent/payment/notice is required) is a standard reservation but, combined with general disclosure, it allows the Seller to disclose a problem for warranty-protection purposes while denying it is a problem.

**Push back:** Disclosure only to the extent it is fair, specific and in sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter. Delete [1.1] and [1.2] general disclosure, or at minimum confine them to matters specifically cross-referenced to the relevant warranty in the Disclosure Letter.

## 5. Buyer knowledge exclusion (Clause 8.3)

"No claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records."

This is a blanket actual-and-constructive knowledge bar. Combined with items 4 and 3, it effectively converts the warranties into a nullity: the Seller discloses everything generally, then says we knew everything disclosed, then says that knowledge bars every claim of any nature.

**Push back:** Delete clause 8.3. If any knowledge qualifier is to survive, it must be (a) limited to actual knowledge, (b) of named buyer individuals, (c) not extend to advisers or "discoverable" matters, and (d) never excuse title, capacity, fraud or any specific indemnity. Separately, any seller knowledge qualifier on warranties should be limited to named seller persons after reasonable enquiry.

## 6. Bluefen consent (Clause 3 / 6.3)

Bluefen is ~AUD 3.6m revenue, ~30% of FY26. The Disclosure Letter at [2] confirms there is **no final written consent and no evidence that the 11.3 conditions are satisfied**. The Seller's draft nonetheless proposes (a) reasonable endeavours only and (b) consent "satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent."

Both are below our playbook. Reasonable endeavours is insufficient for a material customer. "Satisfied on delivery" means a conditional consent, or one whose 11.3 conditions have not been met, would satisfy the condition precedent.

**Push back:** Condition precedent requiring (i) effective written consent from Bluefen under clause 11.2 and (ii) evidence satisfactory to the Buyer that all conditions in clause 11.3 are satisfied, before Completion. Seller obligation at least "all reasonable endeavours" with specific steps. Given 30% revenue concentration, consider whether a Bluefen-specific indemnity or price adjustment is warranted if consent is not obtained on acceptable terms.

## 7. Riverlark facility (Clause 2 / 7)

~AUD 3.2m outstanding; Disclosure Letter [3] confirms no repayment and no discharge of security. The Seller proposes release "following Completion."

This departs from the playbook on every point. A post-completion release means we would acquire the company with AUD 3.2m of secured debt still on foot and the security still registered, reliant on the Seller to procure a release afterwards. That is inconsistent with a debt-free/cash-free deal.

**Push back:** Current payout letter from Riverlark delivered pre-Completion; repayment directly from Completion funds under the funds flow; executed releases of security (and PPSR discharges) delivered at Completion. A post-Completion release is only acceptable with an irrevocable bank undertaking **and** Amelia Frost's written approval, which has not been given.

## 8. Employee bonuses (DD-005, funds flow)

AUD 420,000 of Completion bonuses, conditional on Completion and continued employment. The Seller's position is that these are "a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow." The Disclosure Letter [5] confirms they do not appear in the funds flow and that on-costs (payroll tax, superannuation) are not addressed.

The problem: these are a Company liability triggered by our Completion. If they are not in the funds flow and not treated as Debt, the Company (and therefore we) will pay them after Completion from our money. "A matter for the Seller" is not a mechanism.

**Push back:** Either (a) specific line item in the funds flow deducting AUD 420,000 plus triggered on-costs (superannuation, payroll tax, any leave accruals) from the Seller's proceeds, or (b) express Seller funding of these amounts into the Company before Completion, or (c) treatment as Debt in the completion accounts. We need the Seller to confirm the on-cost position; until then, assume on-costs apply and quantify them.

## 9. Ironquay IP (Clause 11.1)

DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open. No receipt and no confirmatory assignment in the data room. The Seller says the indemnity "limited to the specific SOW3 payment" is adequate.

The exposure is not just the AUD 180,000: if payment has not cleared, the Company may not own the SOW3 deliverables at all. A payment-only indemnity does not cover loss of title to IP, infringement exposure, or the cost of replacement. Note also that under the Seller's draft, this indemnity would be swept into the general cap and 18-month limit (item 3).

We should be careful on the facts: the AUD 180,000 is the Seller's own record and is not independently verified either way. We do not yet know whether it has been paid.

**Push back:** Broaden the indemnity to cover all loss arising from any failure of the Company to own, or to have validly acquired, the SOW3 Project Materials and any related claim by Ironquay, preserving the SOW3 cure mechanism (payment of outstanding fees to perfect transfer). Carve it out of the general regime. Request bank evidence of payment status and, if unpaid, require payment and a confirmatory assignment as a completion deliverable or a specific funds-flow item.

## 10. Export/privacy incident (DD-006, Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6)

~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps) sent via download link to an unintended external address. The Disclosure Letter [6] is fairly drafted: it does not characterise this as a confirmed breach, does not state a loss figure, and confirms the investigation is preliminary. The Seller's SPA position ("preliminary operational matter, not expected to be material") goes further than its own disclosure.

We should not over- or under-state this. There is no confirmed breach, no confirmed harm, no confirmed notification duty. But there is also no evidence that the link was not accessed, and the investigation is incomplete.

**Push back:** Pre-Completion covenants requiring the Seller to (a) preserve all logs and evidence, (b) complete the investigation with appropriate privacy/legal input, (c) provide updates and the final report, and (d) make any notifications that the investigation shows are required. Warranty that the disclosure is complete and accurate. A specific indemnity for loss arising from the DD-006 incident, outside the general cap, is a reasonable ask given it is a known matter; its scope can be negotiated. Do not accept "not expected to be material" as a disclosure characterisation.

## 11. Sandbar supplier renewals (DD-008, DD-011)

Three renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Seller says ordinary-course operating costs. Disclosure Letter [8] says the material does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course, and should be read together for timing/scope.

The playbook is right not to treat this as automatic Debt or an automatic price deduction. The question is factual: are these recurring costs already reflected in the forecasts and working capital, or are they a lump-sum commitment that crystallises around Completion?

**Push back / action:** Request the renewal documents, timing, termination rights and whether any amount is accrued or prepaid. Then decide whether any portion should be treated as Debt, a working capital adjustment, or simply ordinary course. No concession either way at this stage.

## 12. Tax / IP warranties

The Seller "considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above." They are not settled: our playbook records these as OPEN. Folding tax and IP into a 20% cap and 18-month limit would be a material concession, particularly for tax, where assessment periods run well beyond 18 months.

**Push back:** Tax and IP remain open and are separate categories. Do not accept unlimited liability as our position either; the point is simply that they are not resolved and are not part of the general regime.

## 13. Title evidence (DD-012)

The Seller relies on the Company share register at DD-012. The Disclosure Letter [10] candidly admits this "identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification." A share register is a Company-maintained internal document; it is not independent proof of title, absence of encumbrances or Seller authority to sell.

**Push back / action:** Independent verification: ASIC company search, PPSR search against the Company and the shares, constitution and any shareholders' agreement, board/shareholder resolutions of Harbourglass authorising the sale, and the Riverlark security documents (which may charge the shares). Title warranties on a 100%/6-year basis per item 2.

## 14. Lesser items (DD-007 lease, DD-009 Mossvale)

The Disclosure Letter treats both as notification/assignment matters not requiring consent on a share sale. That reading appears reasonable on the face of the disclosure, but we should confirm from the underlying documents that neither contains a change-of-control trigger, and build the lease notification into the completion steps.

---

## Summary of recommendations

**Do not accept the premise.** Reject the "Reviewer Efficiency Note" in writing; nothing is agreed, and every [STANDARD] item is open.

**Hold the liability package at playbook starting positions.** 25% / AUD 6m cap; AUD 5,000 de minimis; AUD 50,000 first-dollar basket; 24 months. No use of the 20% or 18-month fallbacks without Amelia Frost's written authority identifying the draft.

**Rebuild the limitation architecture.** Separate fundamental/title regime (100%, 6+ years, outside basket/de minimis/knowledge). Express, unwaivable fraud/wilful concealment/deliberate misconduct carve-out from everything. Delete "all Claims unless expressly stated" and "any nature" language. Keep Title, Tax, IP, indemnity, payment and covenant categories separate.

**Dismantle the disclosure/knowledge trap.** Specific fair disclosure only; delete general data-room and public-register disclosure; delete clause 8.3.

**Fix the completion mechanics.** Bluefen: effective consent plus evidence of 11.3 conditions, pre-Completion. Riverlark: payout letter, repayment from Completion funds, releases at Completion. Bonuses: AUD 420,000 plus on-costs as a funds-flow line item or Seller-funded.

**Address the known matters specifically.** Ironquay: broader indemnity outside the general cap, preserve the SOW3 cure, verify payment status. DD-006: preservation, investigation, updates, and a specific indemnity; no acceptance of "not material." Sandbar: gather facts before deciding treatment.

**Verify title independently.** ASIC, PPSR, constitution, authority documents. DD-012 is not sufficient.

**Keep Tax and IP open.** Not part of the general regime; not resolved.

**Escalation needed from Amelia Frost (none yet given, so none assumed):** any move to the 20% cap, any move to 18 months, and any post-Completion Riverlark release.

If helpful, I can turn this into a clause-by-clause mark-up or a shorter issues list for the Seller.

This is a blanket actual-and-constructive knowledge bar. Combined with items 4 and 3, it effectively converts the warranties into a nullity: the Seller discloses everything generally, then says we knew everything disclosed, then says that knowledge bars every claim of any nature.

**Push back:** Delete clause 8.3. If any knowledge qualifier is to survive, it must be (a) limited to actual knowledge, (b) of named buyer individuals, (c) not extend to advisers or "discoverable" matters, and (d) never excuse title, capacity, fraud or any specific indemnity. Separately, any seller knowledge qualifier on warranties should be limited to named seller persons after reasonable enquiry.

## 6. Bluefen consent (Clause 3 / 6.3)

Bluefen is ~AUD 3.6m revenue, ~30% of FY26. The Disclosure Letter at [2] confirms there is **no final written consent and no evidence that the 11.3 conditions are satisfied**. The Seller's draft nonetheless proposes (a) reasonable endeavours only and (b) consent "satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent."

Both are below our playbook. Reasonable endeavours is insufficient for a material customer. "Satisfied on delivery" means a conditional consent, or one whose 11.3 conditions have not been met, would satisfy the condition precedent.

**Push back:** Condition precedent requiring (i) effective written consent from Bluefen under clause 11.2 and (ii) evidence satisfactory to the Buyer that all conditions in clause 11.3 are satisfied, before Completion. Seller obligation at least "all reasonable endeavours" with specific steps. Given 30% revenue concentration, consider whether a Bluefen-specific indemnity or price adjustment is warranted if consent is not obtained on acceptable terms.

## 7. Riverlark facility (Clause 2 / 7)

~AUD 3.2m outstanding; Disclosure Letter [3] confirms no repayment and no discharge of security. The Seller proposes release "following Completion."

This departs from the playbook on every point. A post-completion release means we would acquire the company with AUD 3.2m of secured debt still on foot and the security still registered, reliant on the Seller to procure a release afterwards. That is inconsistent with a debt-free/cash-free deal.

**Push back:** Current payout letter from Riverlark delivered pre-Completion; repayment directly from Completion funds under the funds flow; executed releases of security (and PPSR discharges) delivered at Completion. A post-Completion release is only acceptable with an irrevocable bank undertaking **and** Amelia Frost's written approval, which has not been given.

## 8. Employee bonuses (DD-005, funds flow)

AUD 420,000 of Completion bonuses, conditional on Completion and continued employment. The Seller's position is that these are "a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow." The Disclosure Letter [5] confirms they do not appear in the funds flow and that on-costs (payroll tax, superannuation) are not addressed.

The problem: these are a Company liability triggered by our Completion. If they are not in the funds flow and not treated as Debt, the Company (and therefore we) will pay them after Completion from our money. "A matter for the Seller" is not a mechanism.

**Push back:** Either (a) specific line item in the funds flow deducting AUD 420,000 plus triggered on-costs (superannuation, payroll tax, any leave accruals) from the Seller's proceeds, or (b) express Seller funding of these amounts into the Company before Completion, or (c) treatment as Debt in the completion accounts. We need the Seller to confirm the on-cost position; until then, assume on-costs apply and quantify them.

## 9. Ironquay IP (Clause 11.1)

DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open. No receipt and no confirmatory assignment in the data room. The Seller says the indemnity "limited to the specific SOW3 payment" is adequate.

The exposure is not just the AUD 180,000: if payment has not cleared, the Company may not own the SOW3 deliverables at all. A payment-only indemnity does not cover loss of title to IP, infringement exposure, or the cost of replacement. Note also that under the Seller's draft, this indemnity would be swept into the general cap and 18-month limit (item 3).

We should be careful on the facts: the AUD 180,000 is the Seller's own record and is not independently verified either way. We do not yet know whether it has been paid.

**Push back:** Broaden the indemnity to cover all loss arising from any failure of the Company to own, or to have validly acquired, the SOW3 Project Materials and any related claim by Ironquay, preserving the SOW3 cure mechanism (payment of outstanding fees to perfect transfer). Carve it out of the general regime. Request bank evidence of payment status and, if unpaid, require payment and a confirmatory assignment as a completion deliverable or a specific funds-flow item.

## 10. Export/privacy incident (DD-006, Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6)

~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps) sent via download link to an unintended external address. The Disclosure Letter [6] is fairly drafted: it does not characterise this as a confirmed breach, does not state a loss figure, and confirms the investigation is preliminary. The Seller's SPA position ("preliminary operational matter, not expected to be material") goes further than its own disclosure.

We should not over- or under-state this. There is no confirmed breach, no confirmed harm, no confirmed notification duty. But there is also no evidence that the link was not accessed, and the investigation is incomplete.

**Push back:** Pre-Completion covenants requiring the Seller to (a) preserve all logs and evidence, (b) complete the investigation with appropriate privacy/legal input, (c) provide updates and the final report, and (d) make any notifications that the investigation shows are required. Warranty that the disclosure is complete and accurate. A specific indemnity for loss arising from the DD-006 incident, outside the general cap, is a reasonable ask given it is a known matter; its scope can be negotiated. Do not accept "not expected to be material" as a disclosure characterisation.

## 11. Sandbar supplier renewals (DD-008, DD-011)

Three renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Seller says ordinary-course operating costs. Disclosure Letter [8] says the material does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course, and should be read together for timing/scope.

The playbook is right not to treat this as automatic Debt or an automatic price deduction. The question is factual: are these recurring costs already reflected in the forecasts and working capital, or are they a lump-sum commitment that crystallises around Completion?

**Push back / action:** Request the renewal documents, timing, termination rights and whether any amount is accrued or prepaid. Then decide whether any portion should be treated as Debt, a working capital adjustment, or simply ordinary course. No concession either way at this stage.

## 12. Tax / IP warranties

The Seller "considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above." They are not settled: our playbook records these as OPEN. Folding tax and IP into a 20% cap and 18-month limit would be a material concession, particularly for tax, where assessment periods run well beyond 18 months.

**Push back:** Tax and IP remain open and are separate categories. Do not accept unlimited liability as our position either; the point is simply that they are not resolved and are not part of the general regime.

## 13. Title evidence (DD-012)

The Seller relies on the Company share register at DD-012. The Disclosure Letter [10] candidly admits this "identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification." A share register is a Company-maintained internal document; it is not independent proof of title, absence of encumbrances or Seller authority to sell.

**Push back / action:** Independent verification: ASIC company search, PPSR search against the Company and the shares, constitution and any shareholders' agreement, board/shareholder resolutions of Harbourglass authorising the sale, and the Riverlark security documents (which may charge the shares). Title warranties on a 100%/6-year basis per item 2.

## 14. Lesser items (DD-007 lease, DD-009 Mossvale)

The Disclosure Letter treats both as notification/assignment matters not requiring consent on a share sale. That reading appears reasonable on the face of the disclosure, but we should confirm from the underlying documents that neither contains a change-of-control trigger, and build the lease notification into the completion steps.
